query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended as energetic structural materials, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention that could improve ductility and uniform deformability without sacrificing high strength or impact-induced energy release? State the proposed intervention, its hypothesized mechanism, the improvement expected relative to the untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a modest amount of cerium (approximately 5 at.%) to Al0.5NbZrTi1.5Ta0.8 will form a dual-phase microstructure that enhances ductility and uniform deformability without sacrificing its high strength or impact-induced energy release.
generation.material_initial_state: Al0.5NbZrTi1.5Ta0.8 high-entropy alloy produced by vacuum-arc melting that exhibits a predominantly BCC structure with limited ductility and high strength.
generation.intervention: Doping the alloy with approximately 5 at.% cerium (as in the formulation Al0.5NbZrTi1.5Ta0.8Ce0.25).
generation.conditions: Under dynamic compressive loading and impact conditions similar to those used in ballistic penetration tests (e.g., velocities near 700–750 m/s) at ambient temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of localized Ce-rich regions with FCC structure interspersed within the BCC matrix, resulting in dendritic segregation that facilitates dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: Cerium addition promotes the formation of ductile FCC zones that act as plasticity carriers. This microstructural modification enhances strain distribution and delays localization, thus improving ductility and uniform deformability while only modestly reducing the overall yield strength. The energetic characteristics remain largely governed by the matrix composition, preserving impact-induced energy release capability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated alloy, the cerium-doped alloy will exhibit a significant increase in fracture strain (improved ductility) without a critical drop in dynamic compressive strength or energy-release performance during high-velocity impact.
generation.baseline: Al0.5NbZrTi1.5Ta0.8 alloy without cerium addition, characterized by high strength but limited ductility and uniform deformability.
generation.boundary: The improvements are expected to hold under similar processing conditions (vacuum-arc melting with repeated remelting for homogeneity) and within the range of dynamic (impact) testing conditions. Variations in temperature or processing route might affect the balance between phases.
generation.uncertainty: While the evidence supports cerium’s role in enhancing ductility via inducing FCC regions, the precise optimum cerium concentration and the trade-off between slight strength reduction and ductility improvement need further quantification under varied operating and processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Al0.5NbZrTi1.5Ta0.8 alloys with varying cerium contents (0, 5, 10, and 25 at.%). Subject all samples to standardized dynamic compression tests and ballistic penetration tests under identical conditions. Use microstructural analysis (XRD, TEM, SEM-EDS) to correlate the presence of FCC regions and element segregation with mechanical performance.
measurements: Dynamic compressive yield and ultimate strengths
Fracture strain or plasticity levels from high-rate compression tests
Impact-induced energy release (penetration capability and reaction delay time)
Microstructural characterization (phase identification, morphology, and segregation patterns)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cerium-doped alloy at around 5 at.% does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in fracture strain and uniform deformability (or demonstrates unacceptable strength loss or reduced energy-release efficiency) relative to the undoped alloy under identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractEnergetic structural materials play an important role in improving the damage performance of future weapons. To improve the energy-releasing behavior, Al0.5NbZrTi1.5Ta0.8Cex high-entropy alloys were prepared by vacuum-arc melting. The results showed the presence of BCC and FCC phases in the alloy with dendritic-morphology-element segregation and there were significant dislocations in the alloys. The current study focused on the effects of cerium content on the dynamic compressive mechanical and energetic characteristics. Cerium doping enhanced the energy-releasing characteristics of high-entropy alloys. The severity of the reaction increased with the increase in the cerium content, while the dynamic compressive strength generally decreased with the increase in cerium content. The Al0.5NbZrTi1.5Ta0.8Ce0.25 showed excellent mechanical and energy-releasing characteristics. The ballistic experiments indicated that Al0.5NbZrTi1.5Ta0.8Ce0.25 can penetrate 6-millimeter A3 plates and ignite the cotton behind the target at a velocity of 729 m/s, making it an ideal energetic structural material.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, cerium doping, mechanical behavior, energy releasing

Dai’s team analyzed the energy-release process and overpressure of two types of high-entropy alloy fragments, WFeNiMo [] and FeNiCoCr [], in the velocity range, of 500–1800 m/s. It was shown that compared with tungsten alloy, WFeNiMo high-entropy alloy has better energy-releasing characteristics. Ren [] analyzed the mechanism of compression and energy release of TiZrNbV alloy by numerical simulation and experiments. However, the energy-release threshold of the existing high-entropy-alloy energetic-structure materials is relatively high, regardless of whether it is measured by strain rate or impact velocity. Furthermore, chemically active rare-earth elements have not been doped into high-entropy alloys as energetic structural materials. As a rare-earth element, cerium is chemically active. To balance the trade-off between mechanical properties and energetic characteristics, we introduced cerium into the Al0.5NbZrTi1.5Ta0.8 matrix and investigated the effect of cerium content on the dynamic compressive mechanical properties and energy-releasing characteristics of Al0.5NbZrTi1.5Ta0.8Cex high-entropy alloy.

In conclusion, Al0.5NbZrTi1.5Ta0.8Cex the high-entropy alloys prepared by vacuum-arc melting showed excellent compressive mechanical properties and energetic characteristics. The following conclusions can be drawn: The XRD patterns indicate that the matrix had a BCC structure. Cerium doping resulted in the appearance of FCC structure in the alloys. The SEM and EDS illustrated dendritic morphology and element segregation was present in the alloy. The TEM images showed the presence of regions rich in Al, Nb, Zr, Ti and Ta with BCC structures and regions rich in Ce with FCC-structure regions and dislocations in the alloy. The cerium-atom percentage has a significant influence on mechanical properties and energy-releasing behavior. As the cerium-atom percentage increased from 5 at. % to 25 at. %, the dynamic compressive yield strength and ultimate compressive strength showed a generally decreasing trend. The fracture strain of the Ce5 and Ce10 ranged from 9% to 10%, increasing to 19% of the Ce25 because of the continuous Ce-rich regions with FCC structures.
